pages.text: Gulliver's Travels

image.note: Cover: a tiny ship, a giant hand, a small figure

pages.text: Contents. Shipwrecked in Lilliput / Among the Little People / The Land of Giants / Among the Giants / Home Again.

Lemuel Gulliver loved the sea, and the sea took him to the strangest places any traveller ever saw: a land where the people were smaller than your hand, and another where they were taller than a house. Here are his two most famous voyages.

image.note: Gulliver's ship on a wild sea

pages.text: Gulliver was a ship's doctor, and he loved nothing more than a voyage. But on one trip a great storm smashed his ship to pieces, and he swam and swam until, exhausted, he crawled onto a strange beach and fell fast asleep on the grass.

image.note: Gulliver washed ashore, asleep

pages.text: When he woke, he could not move. Not his arms, not his legs, not even his head. Hundreds of tiny threads pinned him to the ground, and his own hair was pegged down. "What is this?" he thought. Then he felt something climbing up his chest.

image.note: Gulliver waking, tied down by threads

pages.text: He turned his eyes downward, and could hardly believe them. A tiny man, no taller than his hand, stood on his chest with a tiny bow, and behind him marched a whole army of little people, each smaller than a mouse, staring up at the giant they had captured.

image.note: A tiny man on Gulliver's chest, army below

pages.text: Gulliver had washed up in Lilliput, a land where everyone was tiny. The little people were terrified of the giant, and had tied him down as he slept. When he roared, they fired tiny arrows like pinpricks, so he lay still and gentle, to show he meant no harm.

image.note: Lilliputians firing tiny arrows

pages.text: Seeing he was peaceful, the Lilliputians grew bold, and kind. They built ramps and carried up baskets of food, and Gulliver ate whole loaves the size of peas by the dozen, and drank barrels like thimbles. Slowly, the tiny people and the giant began to trust one another.

image.note: Lilliputians carrying tiny food to Gulliver

pages.text: They carried him to their city on a great cart pulled by fifteen hundred tiny horses, and there he met their emperor, a proud little man barely as tall as Gulliver's finger, in a helmet no bigger than a coin. The whole city came to gape at the Man-Mountain, as they named him.

image.note: Gulliver meeting the tiny emperor

pages.text: Gulliver tried hard to be a good guest. He let the tiny soldiers march between his legs like an arch. He let children play in his hair. And when a fire broke out in the palace, he put it out in a way only a giant could, though it was not quite the way the queen would have wished.

image.note: Gulliver helping at a tiny palace fire

pages.text: For all their smallness, the Lilliputians had big quarrels. They were at war with a neighbouring land over the terribly important question of which end of a boiled egg one should crack first. Whole battles were fought over it. Gulliver found it very hard not to laugh.

image.note: Two tiny armies arguing over a boiled egg

pages.text: When the enemy fleet sailed to attack, Gulliver simply waded into the sea, which reached only his knees, took hold of all fifty enemy ships by their anchor-ropes, and towed the whole navy back to Lilliput at once. The emperor was overjoyed, and called him the greatest hero in the land.

image.note: Gulliver wading, towing a tiny fleet

pages.text: But favour is a slippery thing. The more the emperor asked, the more his jealous advisers whispered that the Man-Mountain was too powerful, too hungry, too dangerous to keep. Slowly the mood turned, and Gulliver heard that they meant to do him harm.

image.note: Advisers whispering, plotting

pages.text: So one quiet morning, before they could act, Gulliver waded across to the neighbouring land, found a real boat washed up on the shore, big enough even for him, and set sail for home. He left the tiny kingdom behind, and it must be said, he was not entirely sorry to go.

image.note: Gulliver sailing away from Lilliput

pages.text: You might think Gulliver had learned his lesson about the sea. He had not. Before long he was off again, and this time a different accident left him alone on a strange shore. But here everything was turned upside down. Here, it was Gulliver who was tiny.

image.note: Gulliver small in a giant landscape

pages.text: The grass towered over his head like trees. When a farmer walked by, his footsteps shook the ground like thunder, and his boots were the size of houses. This was Brobdingnag, the land of giants, and Gulliver was now the little one, no taller than a giant's hand.

image.note: Giant farmer beside tiny Gulliver

pages.text: The farmer found him and, gently, picked him up between finger and thumb, and carried him home like a curious insect. Gulliver was terrified, but the farmer meant no harm. He set him on the table, where the whole family stared at the tiny talking man in wonder.

image.note: Tiny Gulliver on a giant table

pages.text: The farmer's young daughter, a kind girl named Glumdalclitch, took Gulliver into her care. She made him a little bed in a doll's cradle, sewed him tiny clothes, and kept him safe. To her he was the most precious thing in the world, and she was, to him, a gentle giant nurse.

image.note: Giant girl making a bed for tiny Gulliver

pages.text: But a world of giants is a dangerous place when you are tiny. A house cat looked to Gulliver like a monster. A wasp was the size of a bird, and its sting a spear. Once a naughty monkey snatched him up and carried him along the rooftops, until he was rescued, shaken but safe.

image.note: A giant wasp menacing tiny Gulliver

pages.text: The giants, though, were mostly gentle, and terribly amused by him. The farmer, seeing money to be made, showed Gulliver off in the towns, until the tiny man was worn out with performing. At last word reached the palace, and the queen herself bought him, to Glumdalclitch's joy, for she came too.

image.note: Gulliver performing on a tiny stage for giants

pages.text: At court, Gulliver told the giant king all about his own country: its wars, its guns, its clever machines, quite proud of it all. But the wise old king only frowned. "How strange," he said, "that such tiny creatures should think of so many ways to harm one another." Gulliver had no answer to that.

image.note: Tiny Gulliver on the giant king's palm

pages.text: Gulliver lived long among the giants, safe with Glumdalclitch, a tiny wonder in a huge world. Then one day, by the sea, a great bird snatched up the box he slept in and dropped it, splash, into the ocean, where a passing ship, an ordinary ship of ordinary size, found it and hauled it aboard.

image.note: A bird dropping Gulliver's box into the sea

pages.text: When the sailors opened the box and a small man climbed out talking of giants, they thought him quite mad, for to them he was ordinary-sized, and there were no giants to be seen. It took Gulliver a long time to feel the right size again in an ordinary world.

image.note: Gulliver climbing from the box among sailors

pages.text: Gulliver had other voyages too: to a floating island in the sky, and to a land where horses were wise and ruled themselves. But his two strangest lessons came from Lilliput and Brobdingnag: that a giant among small folk, and a small man among giants, are really the very same person. Only the world around them has changed.

image.note: Gulliver home, remembering giant and tiny both

pages.text: "Big and small," Gulliver would say, "are not always what they seem. I have been a mountain and I have been a mouse, and I was Gulliver all along." And with that, though he swore each time he would never sail again, he would look at the sea, and begin, quietly, to pack.

image.note: Gulliver by the shore, bag packed, eyeing the sea

pages.text: Gulliver's voyages. Lilliput: where the people are tiny, and their quarrels tinier still. Brobdingnag: where the giants are huge, and one small man learns how the world looks from below. Two lands, one traveller, and a great deal to think about.
